Using Sums-of-Squares to Prove Gaussian Product Inequalities

Oliver Russell    Wei Sun Affiliation: Department of Mathematics and Statistics Affiliation: Concordia University, Canada Email: o_russel@live.concordia.ca, wei.sun@concordia.ca
Abstract

The long-standing Gaussian product inequality (GPI) conjecture states that E⁡[∏j=1nXj2​mj]≥∏j=1nE⁡[Xj2​mj]E[\prod_{j=1}^{n}X_{j}^{2m_{j}}]\geq\prod_{j=1}^{n}E[X_{j}^{2m_{j}}] for any centered Gaussian random vector (X1,…,Xn)(X_{1},\dots,X_{n}) and m1,…,mn∈ℕm_{1},\dots,m_{n}\in\mathbb{N}. In this paper, we describe a computational algorithm involving sums-of-squares representations of multivariate polynomials that can be used to resolve the GPI conjecture. To exhibit the power of this novel method, we apply it to prove two new GPIs: E⁡[X12​m1​X26​X34]≥E⁡[X12​m1]​E​[X26]​E​[X34]E[X_{1}^{2m_{1}}X_{2}^{6}X_{3}^{4}]\geq E[X_{1}^{2m_{1}}]E[X_{2}^{6}]E[X_{3}^{4}] and E⁡[X12​m1​X22​X32​X42]≥E⁡[X12​m1]​E​[X22]​E​[X32]​E​[X42]E[X_{1}^{2m_{1}}X_{2}^{2}X_{3}^{2}X_{4}^{2}]\geq E[X_{1}^{2m_{1}}]E[X_{2}^{2}]E[X_{3}^{2}]E[X_{4}^{2}].

MSC: Primary 60E15; Secondary 62H12

Keywords: Moments of Gaussian random vector, Gaussian product inequality conjecture, sums-of-squares, semi-definite programming.

1 Introduction

Gaussian distributions play a fundamental role in both probability and statistics (see [19] and references therein). Over the past decade, there has been a surge of interest in the study of inequalities related to Gaussian distributions. This was sparked by Royen’s famous proof of the long-conjectured Gaussian correlation inequality (GCI) [15, 9]. Gaussian inequalities are valuable tools to the study of small ball probabilities (see, for example, Li [10] and Shao [17]) and the zeros of random polynomials (see, for example, Li and Shao [11]), among others. In this paper, we will investigate the Gaussian product inequality (GPI), another long-standing conjecture and one of the late Wenbo Li’s open problems (see Shao [18]).

In its most general form, the GPI conjecture (see Li and Wei [12]) states that for any non-negative real numbers αj\alpha_{j}, j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,{n}, and any n{n}-dimensional real-valued centered Gaussian random vector (X1,…,Xn)(X_{1},\dots,X_{n}),

E⁡[∏j=1n|Xj|αj]≥∏j=1nE⁡[|Xj|αj].\displaystyle E\left[\prod_{j=1}^{n}|X_{j}|^{\alpha_{j}}\right]\geq\prod_{j=1}^{n}E[|X_{j}|^{\alpha_{j}}]. (1.1)

Verification of this inequality has immediate and far-reaching consequences. For example (see Malicet et al. [13]), if (1.1) holds when the αj\alpha_{j}’s are any equal positive even integers, then the ‘real linear polarization constant’ conjecture raised by Benítem et al. [1] is true, and (1.1) is deeply linked to the celebrated UU-conjecture by Kagan, Linnik and Rao [7].

The GPI conjecture has proven very challenging to solve, but not for lack of trying. Some progress has been made in the form of partial results. In [4], Frenkel used algebraic methods to prove (1.1) for the case that αj=2\alpha_{j}=2 for each j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,{n}. In [8, Theorem 3.2], Lan et al. used the Gaussian hypergeometric functions to prove the following GPI: for any m1,m2∈ℕm_{1},m_{2}\in\mathbb{N} and any centered Gaussian random vector (X1,X2,X3)(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3}),

E⁡[X12​m1​X22​m2​X32​m2]≥E⁡[X12​m1]​E​[X22​m2]​E​[X32​m2].E[X_{1}^{2m_{1}}X_{2}^{2m_{2}}X_{3}^{2m_{2}}]\geq E[X_{1}^{2m_{1}}]E[X_{2}^{2m_{2}}]E[X_{3}^{2m_{2}}].

Lan et al.’s proof of the 33-dimensional GPI brought renewed hope to solving this difficult problem.

Throughout this paper, any Gaussian random variable is assumed to be real-valued and non-degenerate, i.e., has positive variance. We will study the following conjecture.

Conjecture 1.1

Let n≥3n\geq 3 and m1,…,mn∈ℕm_{1},\dots,m_{n}\in\mathbb{N}. For any centered Gaussian random vector (X1,…,Xn)(X_{1},\dots,X_{n}),

E⁡[∏j=1nXj2​mj]≥∏j=1nE⁡[Xj2​mj].E\left[\prod_{j=1}^{n}X_{j}^{2m_{j}}\right]\geq\prod_{j=1}^{n}E[X_{j}^{2m_{j}}]. (1.2)

The equality holds if and only if X1,…,XnX_{1},\dots,X_{n} are independent.

Most recently, using combinatorial methods we proved Conjecture 1.1 for n=3n=3 when m1=1,m2=2,m3∈ℕm_{1}=1,m_{2}=2,m_{3}\in\mathbb{N} and m1=1,m2=3,m3∈ℕm_{1}=1,m_{2}=3,m_{3}\in\mathbb{N} (see [16, Theorem 3.5]). In addition, in the same paper, we proved the GPI (for any n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}) when all correlations are non-negative.

Proposition 1.2

([16, Lemma 2.3]) Let (X1,…,Xn)(X_{1},\dots,X_{n}) be a centered Gaussian random vector such that E⁡[Xi​Xj]≥0E[X_{i}X_{j}]\geq 0 for any i≠ji\not=j. Then, (1.2) holds and

E⁡[∏j=1nXj2​mj]≥E⁡[∏j=1kXj2​mj]​E​[∏j=k+1nXj2​mj],∀1≤k≤n−1.\displaystyle E\left[\prod_{j=1}^{n}X_{j}^{2m_{j}}\right]\geq E\left[\prod_{j=1}^{k}X_{j}^{2m_{j}}\right]E\left[\prod_{j=k+1}^{n}X_{j}^{2m_{j}}\right],\ \ \ \ \forall 1\leq k\leq n-1.
Remark 1.3

(i) Genest and Ouimet [5] proved that (1.2) holds under the assumption that there exists a matrix C∈[0,∞)n×nC\in[0,\infty)^{n\times n} such that (X1,…,Xn)=(U1,…,Un)​C(X_{1},\dots,X_{n})=(U_{1},\dots,U_{n})C in law, where (U1,…,Un)(U_{1},\dots,U_{n}) is an nn-dimensional standard Gaussian random vector. Recently, Edelmann et al. [3] used a different method to extend [16, Lemma 2.3] to the multivariate gamma distribution. It is interesting to point out that Edelmann et al. [3] also demonstrated a strong connection between the GCI and the GPI.

(ii) Note that the product inequality (1.2) may not hold for non-Gaussian random vectors. Let V1V_{1} and V2V_{2} be independent Rademacher random variables, i.e., P⁡(Vi=1)=P⁡(Vi=−1)=12P(V_{i}=1)=P(V_{i}=-1)=\frac{1}{2}, i=1,2i=1,2. Define Y1=V1+0.9​V2Y_{1}=V_{1}+0.9V_{2} and Y2=V1−0.9​V2Y_{2}=V_{1}-0.9V_{2}. Then, (Y1,Y2)(Y_{1},Y_{2}) is a centered random vector with

Cov⁡(Y1,Y2)=E⁡[V12−0.81​V22]=0.19.{\rm Cov}(Y_{1},Y_{2})=E[V_{1}^{2}-0.81V_{2}^{2}]=0.19.

We have

E⁡[Y12​Y22]=E⁡[(V12−0.81​V22)2]=(0.19)2,E[Y_{1}^{2}Y_{2}^{2}]=E[(V_{1}^{2}-0.81V_{2}^{2})^{2}]=(0.19)^{2},

and

E⁡[Y12]​E​[Y22]=(1.81)2.E[Y_{1}^{2}]E[Y_{2}^{2}]=(1.81)^{2}.

Hence

E⁡[Y12​Y22]<E⁡[Y12]​E​[Y22].E[Y_{1}^{2}Y_{2}^{2}]<E[Y_{1}^{2}]E[Y_{2}^{2}].

In this paper, we develop an efficient computational algorithm that produces exact sums-of-squares (SOS) polynomials to tackle the GPI. We describe this method in Section 2 and use it to rigorously prove two previously unsolved special cases of the GPI conjecture with fixed exponents in Section 3. Then, in Section 4, we reveal the true power of the SOS method by extending these special cases to the stronger result where one exponent is unbounded. Fully solving the GPI conjecture is most difficult when correlations can be negative. In theory, our algorithm is applicable to any GPI of the form (1.2) with dimension and all but one exponent fixed, and is therefore the first universal method for solving the GPI.

2 The SOS method of solving the GPI

An SOS representation of a polynomial is of the form ∑i=1pfi2\sum_{i=1}^{p}f_{i}^{2}, where the fif_{i}’s are real-coefficient polynomials. It is clear that any polynomial with an SOS representation is necessarily non-negative.

Lemma 2.1

Let (X1,…,Xn)(X_{1},\dots,X_{n}) be a centered Gaussian random vector. Denote by Λ\Lambda the covariance matrix of (X1,…,Xn)(X_{1},\dots,X_{n}) and cm1,…,mnc_{m_{1},\dots,m_{n}} the coefficient corresponding to the term t12​m1⋯tn2​mnt_{1}^{2m_{1}}\cdots t_{n}^{2m_{n}} of the polynomial

G⁡(t1,…,tn)=(∑k,l=1nΛk​l​tk​tl)∑j=1nmj,t1,…,tn∈ℝ.G(t_{1},\dots,t_{n})=\left(\sum_{k,l=1}^{n}\Lambda_{kl}t_{k}t_{l}\right)^{\sum_{j=1}^{n}m_{j}},\ \ \ \ t_{1},\dots,t_{n}\in\mathbb{R}.

Then,

E⁡[∏j=1nXj2​mj]=∏j=1n(2​mj)!2∑j=1nmj​(∑j=1nmj)!⋅cm1,…,mn.E\left[\prod_{j=1}^{n}X_{j}^{2m_{j}}\right]=\frac{\prod_{j=1}^{n}(2m_{j})!}{2^{\sum_{j=1}^{n}m_{j}}(\sum_{j=1}^{n}m_{j})!}\cdot c_{m_{1},\dots,m_{n}}. (2.1)

(2.3)

Combining (2.2) and (2.3), we have an algorithm to get the expression of
Fm1,…,mn​(x11,…,x1​n,…,xn​1,…,xn​n)F_{m_{1},\dots,m_{n}}(x_{11},\dots,x_{1n},\dots,x_{n1},\dots,x_{nn}). Suppose we consider (2.3) for fixed n,m1,…,mnn,m_{1},\dots,m_{n}. Applying the Macaulay2 package ‘SumsOfSquares’ [2] to this polynomial, we may attempt to obtain an SOS decomposition ∑i=1pci​fi2\sum_{i=1}^{p}c_{i}f_{i}^{2} of Fm1,…,mnF_{m_{1},\dots,m_{n}}, where the cic_{i}’s are positive rational numbers and the fif_{i}’s are rational-coefficient polynomials. Although it is still an open problem whether or not every rational-coefficient SOS polynomial necessarily has such a decomposition, this software aims to produce one regardless (see Peyrl and Parrilo [14]). If it is obtained, then (1.2) is verified for this case.

This package is very user-friendly and, along with the semi-definite programming package it uses, comes pre-installed in the newest versions of Macaulay2. By using a “mixed symbolic-numerical approach” [14], ‘SumsOfSquares’ takes advantage of the speed of approximate numerical calculations, yet still produces a final SOS decomposition that is exact (not an approximation). This SOS polynomial can then be expanded and checked to match the original Fm1,…,mnF_{m_{1},\dots,m_{n}} using the value() function.

To further increase the efficiency of our method, we will use a trick to reduce the degree of the polynomial Fm1,…,mnF_{m_{1},\dots,m_{n}}. In this way, calculation of the SOS decomposition becomes significantly less computationally intensive and much faster. This technique resides in a key result proved in our previous paper which we restate here for convenience.

Lemma 2.2

([16, Lemma 2.1]) Let n≥3n\geq 3 and m1,…,mn∈ℕm_{1},\dots,m_{n}\in\mathbb{N}. If for any centered Gaussian random vector (Y1,…,Yn)(Y_{1},\dots,Y_{n}) with Yn=α1​Y1+⋯+αn−1​Yn−1Y_{n}=\alpha_{1}Y_{1}+\cdots+\alpha_{n-1}Y_{n-1} for some constants α1,…,αn−1\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{n-1},

E⁡[{∏j=1n−1Yj2​mj}​Yn2​k]≥{∏j=1n−1E⁡[Yj2​mj]}​E​[Yn2​k], 0≤k≤mn,E\left[\left\{\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}Y_{j}^{2m_{j}}\right\}Y_{n}^{2k}\right]\geq\left\{\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}E[Y_{j}^{2m_{j}}]\right\}E[Y_{n}^{2k}],\ \ \ \ 0\leq k\leq m_{n}, (2.4)

then for any centered Gaussian random vector (X1,…,Xn)(X_{1},\dots,X_{n}),

E⁡[∏j=1nXj2​mj]≥∏j=1nE⁡[Xj2​mj].E\left[\prod_{j=1}^{n}X_{j}^{2m_{j}}\right]\geq\prod_{j=1}^{n}E[X_{j}^{2m_{j}}]. (2.5)

Additionally, if inequality (2.4) is strict when k=mnk=m_{n}, then the equality sign of (2.5) holds only if XnX_{n} is independent of X1,…,Xn−1X_{1},\dots,X_{n-1}.

To establish the inequality (3.1), we need only consider Case 1. However, to show that the equality sign holds if and only if X1,X2,X3,X4X_{1},X_{2},X_{3},X_{4} are independent, we must check all three cases.

4 The SOS method with one exponent unbounded

In this section, we demonstrate an even more powerful application of the SOS method to be used when one exponent is unknown. In particular, we extend Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 to the case where m1m_{1} is unbounded by exploiting the fact that verifying these GPIs can be reduced to proving the non-negativity of a multivariate polynomial with variables a,b,…,m1a,b,...,m_{1}.

Theorem 4.1

Let m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}. For any centered Gaussian random vector (X1,X2,X3)(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3}),

X1=U1,X2=aU1+U2,X3=bU1+U2,a,b∈ℝ.X_{1}=U_{1},\,\,X_{2}=aU_{1}+U_{2},\,\,X_{3}=bU_{1}+U_{2},\,\,\,a,b\in\mathbb{R}.

Remark 4.3

To establish the inequality (4.1), we need only consider Case 1. However, to show that the equality sign holds if and only if X1,X2,X3,X4X_{1},X_{2},X_{3},X_{4} are independent, we must check all three cases.

5 Discussion

The GPI conjecture is an extremely difficult problem to solve, particularly when some of the correlations are negative. The SOS method described in this paper can be used to rigorously verify any specific case of the GPI, constrained only by computing power. Furthermore, as demonstrated in Section 4, this method is even powerful enough to prove GPIs with one exponent unbounded, a feat that is extremely difficult by purely theoretical methods (cf. [16, Theorem 3.5]). On the other hand, should the GPI conjecture not hold in its full generality, our method may prove quite useful in the search for a counterexample. Our algorithm is efficient, straightforward and produces exact results. Furthermore, whereas calculations of multivariate Gaussian moments are often burdened by the constraints imposed by the covariance matrix, our method has the advantage of using free variables (with domain over the reals).

Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 constitute never-before obtained results. In fact, we were able to verify many more GPIs with one exponent unbounded and higher fixed exponents, the proofs of which we omit seeing as the SOS decompositions, although exact, can be quite long. In view of these new GPI affirmations, we propose a stronger version of the GPI:

Conjecture 5.1

Let n≥3n\geq 3, m1,…,mn∈ℕm_{1},\dots,m_{n}\in\mathbb{N}, and U1,…,UnU_{1},\dots,U_{n} be independent standard Gaussian random variables. Define the polynomial HH on ℝn⁡(n−1)/2\mathbb{R}^{n(n-1)/2} by

H⁡(x21,x31,x32,…,xn​1,…,xn,n−1)\displaystyle H(x_{21},x_{31},x_{32},\dots,x_{n1},\dots,x_{n,n-1})
=\displaystyle= E⁡[U12​m1​∏i=2n(∑j=1i−1xi​j​Uj+Ui)2​mi]−(2​m1−1)!!​∏i=2nE⁡[(∑j=1i−1xi​j​Uj+Ui)2​mi].\displaystyle E\left[U_{1}^{2m_{1}}\prod_{i=2}^{n}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}x_{ij}U_{j}+U_{i}\right)^{2m_{i}}\right]-(2m_{1}-1)!!\prod_{i=2}^{n}E\left[\left(\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}x_{ij}U_{j}+U_{i}\right)^{2m_{i}}\right].

Then, HH has an SOS representation.

By approximation, we find that if Conjecture 5.1 is true then the GPI (1.2) holds. By virtue of this conjecture, we have connected the probability inequality to analysis, algebra, geometry, combinatorics, mathematical programming and computer science.

It is well-known that a non-negative multivariate polynomial may not have an SOS representation. Denote by Pn,2​dP_{n,2d} the set of all non-negative polynomials in nn variables of degree at most 2​d2d and ∑n,2​d\sum_{n,2d} the set of all polynomials in Pn,2​dP_{n,2d} that are SOS. In 1888, Hilbert proved that ∑n,2​d=Pn,2​d\sum_{n,2d}=P_{n,2d} if and only if n=1n=1 or d=1d=1 or (n,d)=(2,2)(n,d)=(2,2) (see [6]). However, we would like to point out that E⁡[∏j=1nXj2​mj]E\left[\prod_{j=1}^{n}X_{j}^{2m_{j}}\right] itself is an SOS. To see this, let U1,…,UnU_{1},\dots,U_{n} be independent standard Gaussian random variables. For x11,…,x1​n,…,xn​1,…,xn​n∈ℝx_{11},\dots,x_{1n},\dots,x_{n1},\dots,x_{nn}\in\mathbb{R}, we can write:

Xi=∑j=1nxi​j​Uj, 1≤i≤n.X_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{ij}U_{j},\ \ \ \ 1\leq i\leq n.

Then, we have

∏j=1nXj2​mj=a′​b,\prod_{j=1}^{n}X_{j}^{2m_{j}}=a^{\prime}b,

where a′=(1,x11,…,xn​n,x112,x11x12,…,x1​nm1⋯xn​nmn)a^{\prime}=(1,x_{11},\dots,x_{nn},x_{11}^{2},x_{11}x_{12},\dots,x_{1n}^{m_{1}}\cdots x_{nn}^{m_{n}}) is a vector of monomials of length l≤n∑j=1nmjl\leq n^{\sum_{j=1}^{n}m_{j}} and b′=(P1​(U1,…,Un),P2​(U1,…,Un),…,Pl​(U1,…,Un))b^{\prime}=(P_{1}(U_{1},\dots,U_{n}),P_{2}(U_{1},\dots,U_{n}),\dots,P_{l}(U_{1},\dots,U_{n})) is a vector of polynomials also of length ll. Thus,

E⁡[∏j=1nXj2​mj]=E⁡[(∏j=1nXjmj)2]=E⁡[a′​b​b′​a]=a′​Q​a,E\left[\prod_{j=1}^{n}X_{j}^{2m_{j}}\right]=E\left[\left(\prod_{j=1}^{n}X_{j}^{m_{j}}\right)^{2}\right]=E[a^{\prime}bb^{\prime}a]=a^{\prime}Qa,

where Q=b​b′Q=bb^{\prime} is a non-negative definite matrix. Therefore, E⁡[∏j=1nXj2​mj]E\left[\prod_{j=1}^{n}X_{j}^{2m_{j}}\right] has an SOS representation.
